data.title: The Most Famous Problem in Math Was Just Solved by AI-and This Human — WSJ
data.description:
By Ben Cohen and Joshua Robinson

Levent Alpöge has a résumé that would impress even Claude.

He graduated Harvard with the highest GPA in his class, won the prize for America's top young math researcher and earned his Ph.D. in math from Princeton before he took a job at Anthropic. He also speaks six languages and hopes to add Latin and ancient Greek.

And he recently had a work experience that had never before appeared on anyone's CV: He believes he's solved the single most famous problem in all of mathematics.

Ever since 1859, when Bernhard Riemann hypothesized about the pattern of prime numbers, mathematicians had tried, failed and gone mad trying to prove his conjecture. But last week, Alpöge felt that he and Anthropic's Claude were closing in on math's holy grail. Days before his company's trillion-dollar IPO, he fired off a message to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.

"Hypothetically," Alpöge says he began, "if I were to have..."

The day after Anthropic went public, he went public with his secret. Alpöge and AI had discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

Once he published it, mathematicians around the world scrambled to verify his proof's code — all 17 million lines of it. The next day, two independent groups announced they had "full confidence" it was correct. "We congratulate him on this achievement," they wrote.

If it holds up to further scrutiny, the achievement would make the 34-year-old employee of an AI company one of the most prominent mathematicians in history — the man who solved Riemann.

It also appears to be the most dazzling example yet of humans and AI pushing the frontier of knowledge.

Many in the math world see Alpöge and Claude's breakthrough as a preview of "centaur science," in which humans work together with their machines to make discoveries that neither could have accomplished on their own.

Anthropic declined to comment and didn't make Alpöge available to comment beyond his papers and social-media posts.

In his own telling, Alpöge is an "old-school mathematician" who just so happens to be working on the bleeding edge of the field. He combines his taste, intuition and expertise with absurdly powerful technology to produce unfathomable results.

This one seemed especially improbable. Until recently, some forecasters predicted the Riemann Hypothesis would stand until 2035. Terence Tao, widely considered the world's finest mathematician, theorized last month that humans and AI might be able to conquer it by 2050.

Alpöge was ahead of schedule, but he always has been. Born in New York to Turkish parents, he was a precocious child whose mother noticed him reading at 3 years old. He learned arithmetic from his sister in the back seat during long car rides. Even then, his brain worked in unusual ways. Alpöge says he has synesthesia, which means he experiences letters and numbers in color.

As a high-school student on Long Island, he used Nvidia's graphics processing units to analyze medical scans long before those chips would power the AI boom. He was selected as a finalist in the Intel Science Talent Search, which came with the nerdiest possible reward: putting his name on an asteroid now known as 25898 Alpoge.

Back on this planet, he went to Harvard and graduated in 2014 with a bachelor's in math and a master's in physics. In his spare time, he woke up at 5 a.m. and trained for marathons. He also finished at the very top of his class.

After graduation, he told CNN Türk what he wanted to do with the rest of his life.

"My dream," he said, "is to solve the Riemann Hypothesis."

While every mathematician dreams of solving Riemann, few were better positioned to actually do it. At summer research programs in college, Alpöge gravitated to hard problems and stood out for his ability to simplify the complex into elegant work. In a letter of recommendation, Williams College professor Steven J. Miller wrote: "Of all the students I have known, he has the greatest potential to be a leader in mathematics."

Along the way, Alpöge studied number theory, probability and combinatorics before writing a prizewinning thesis with an epigraph from a different 19th-century German mathematician: "God made the integers; all else is the work of man." ("It's always been clear that he's very passionate about math," said his adviser Jacob Tsimerman, who recently won the Fields Medal, math's top honor, and pivoted to AI safety.)

His work earned Alpöge a scholarship to Cambridge, a spot at Princeton for his Ph.D. and an elite fellowship back on Harvard's campus. But when OpenAI released its GPT-4 model in 2023, he saw the future of math and left academia for AI.

"To me," he later wrote, "it was instantly the most interesting thing humanity had ever created."

In 2024, he started at Anthropic to work on AI — and with AI.

And it was in 2026 that Alpöge emerged as a main character in the math wars.

This summer, he became a frenetic presence on X, where he made a habit of dropping major results without any of the decorum his peers expected. On a Sunday night in July, he tweeted, "hello there the jacobian conjecture is false," announcing that Anthropic's top model found a counterexample to the 87-year-old riddle of algebraic geometry that day, while billions of humans were busy watching the World Cup final.

On Aug. 31, he seized the attention of the math world again with two words: Augustus Mirabilis.

At OpenAI, his cryptic tweet was taken to mean that something amazing had just happened: Anthropic must have solved a Millennium Prize Problem.

In 2000, seven notoriously difficult problems were designated as math's greatest challenges and each was given a bounty of $1 million. Only one had ever been cracked.

But after Alpöge's tweet, amid rumors that Anthropic was on the verge of a solution, and perhaps two, OpenAI launched its own bid for glory. On Sept. 1, the company unleashed a powerful model and millions of dollars in computing resources on a bunch of math problems. A week later, OpenAI unveiled its solution to the Navier-Stokes problem. For a year, Alpöge had been quietly working on the same one with an NYU mathematician, and the landmark proof set off a vicious fight for credit — with Alpöge caught in the middle.

In October, mathematicians were still reeling from the Millennium Prize brawl when OpenAI released not just one result but hundreds at the same time. Alpöge himself called it "obviously the most significant moment in mathematical history."

At least for a little while longer.

After all the extraordinary advances this year, the biggest prize was still out there: a resolution of Riemann's hypothesis on the mysterious distribution of primes, a topic that has captivated mathematicians for millennia. Alpöge had obsessed over it since childhood. In school, he familiarized himself with the tools he might need to tackle it. He figured he had decades.

As it turns out, he miscalculated.

Alpöge hasn't revealed his prompts or his compute budget, so it remains unclear exactly who did what. But it's clear that Claude wasn't working autonomously. Alpöge's years of preparation and deep understanding of Riemann allowed him to steer the model in the right direction. "Claude and I," he wrote, "had a great time together."

Alpöge acknowledges that he doesn't yet understand all of the math in his own proof and he's trying to digest it along with other humans. But as it came into view, he pulled all-nighters and watched his collaborator in awe.

"Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," he wrote. "Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."

What Claude could not do was write. When Alpöge asked it to put the proof into words, he said the AI churned out 250,000 pages of what he called an "unreadable travesty of 'slop.'"

The other problem with this solution to a 167-year-old problem was the timing: Anthropic was days away from the largest initial public offering in history.

"If I could have," he wrote, "I'd have finished this all much earlier."

Alpöge held off posting it until the day after the company went public. That morning, he published the proof's code on his personal website along with a four-page file called "remark.pdf."

It was the most impressive achievement on his résumé — and one that mathematicians had chased for more than a century.

"I just could not live," he wrote, "if I waited even longer."

data.title: The Latest Chapter in Corporate America's Rocky History With Boardroom Romance — WSJ
data.description:
By Lindsay Ellis and Allison Pohle

Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia Monday to literal cheers from his own employees and quips of satisfaction from the business leaders who supported him.

Bill Ackman, chief executive of Pershing Square, wrote on X, "The wisdom of the crowd prevails." Elon Musk added, "The mistake has been corrected." Sam Altman, whose own ouster as OpenAI's CEO three years ago ended in a return days later, posted an upbeat "Jensen!"

But there was another group of American executives, board members and their advisers who were grappling with what precedent this sets for corporate governance and leadership amid scandal. Huang's return followed advocacy from President Trump, pleas from employees and a major selloff that wiped out more than $2 trillion in Nvidia's market capitalization.

Former Baxter International CEO Harry Kraemer Jr. said he quickly started fielding text messages and calls from former colleagues. Kraemer, who now teaches management at Northwestern University's business school, said he kept coming back to one question: "What is the message that's sent to every other CEO in the U.S.?"

Huang resigned after two extramarital affairs — one with a subordinate and another with a customer, whom U.S. officials believed was working with Chinese intelligence.

Admitted missteps and allegations of misconduct have toppled executives at public giants and flashy startups. Relationships with colleagues have cost McDonald's Steve Easterbrook, BP's Bernard Looney and Norfolk Southern's Alan Shaw their jobs. The Astronomer CEO Andy Byron had to resign after he was caught on the Coldplay kiss-cam with another company executive.

Silicon Valley has long had a tension between the rules intended to protect workers and an entrenched idea of a "brilliant, disruptive leader," said Margaret O'Mara, a historian of the technology industry at the University of Washington. "If there's a tone set at the top of tolerating certain actions, managerial behavior, that's the culture of the company."

Rather than slinking into the background, Huang pressed his case, she said, adding that his reinstatement may set a precedent for other boards.

On Monday, surrounded by Nvidia employees who chanted "Jen-sen," "Jen-sen," Huang said: "I'm going to be a better CEO the second time around."

Central to Huang's comeback is an air of irreplaceability, leadership experts said. He had dozens of direct reports, no obvious successor, a deep relationship with Trump and led a company that acted as the cornerstone of the global artificial-intelligence transition.

His departure — and return — is a warning to boards to not let one executive become indispensable, these experts said.

The reinstatement makes a mockery of company policy, says Charles Elson, a former board member at Sunbeam Corp., AutoZone and others, and the founding director of the University of Delaware's Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance. "You can't have one person subject to the policy and someone else not — they're all employees."

This dynamic is an issue of sound management — or lack thereof, Elson says. Someone will always come along and say the genius needs to stay. But what happens if said genius dies or gets sick, or isn't a genius any longer, he says: "It is really poor, in my view, business management."

Nvidia didn't immediately reply to a request for comment.

Board leaders and corporate advisers are quick to note that leaders' ability to hold on to their jobs reflects circumstances distinctive to each situation, and urged caution in extrapolating a new normal in governance from the Huang return.

Employees watch what companies reward, as well as what they tolerate and hold accountable, says Irina Wolpert, who leads the Americas FinTech practice at Egon Zehnder. "When a uniquely consequential leader is treated differently, the board has to be particularly clear about the principles behind that decision and how those principles connect to the culture it wants to sustain."

The situation harks back to 2008 with "too big to fail" parallels, says Peter Gleason, chief executive of the National Association of Corporate Directors. Nvidia's stock affects not only the U.S. stock market, but the global economy as well, he said.

Even still, board directors need to maintain independence. Founder-led chief executives are rare in the world of public companies, Gleason says, but succession planning is one of the board's top responsibilities, and not having a plan in place is itself a crisis.

"I think this is going to be a case study for years to come," he says.

data.title: The Frantic White House Push to Get Jensen Huang Back — WSJ
data.description:
By Amrith Ramkumar, Josh Dawsey, C. Ryan Barber and Robbie Whelan

WASHINGTON — The artificial-intelligence boom that had powered the U.S. stock market and economy for months was coming undone.

Jensen Huang, the longtime CEO of chipmaking giant Nvidia, had been ousted following revelations of two affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Investors were hitting sell on the entire AI trade.

President Trump told associates there was only one solution: getting Huang, a friend and ally, his job back.

Over the weekend, Attorney General Todd Blanche presented an opening. The nation's top law enforcement officer informed Trump and Vice President JD Vance on Saturday that Huang wasn't the target or the subject of any Justice Department investigation, adding that the department had no evidence to suggest that he had broken laws or was a national security risk, according to U.S. officials.

It was an extraordinary effort to clear the name of a man who had been tainted by intelligence reports that were circulated at the highest levels of government.

Underpinning Blanche's assessment was Nvidia's months of cooperation during Huang's leadership with Justice Department investigations into suspected smuggling of powerful artificial intelligence chips by two of the company's customers into China, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.

What followed was a frantic 48 hours in which the president, the vice president and other top administration officials relayed Blanche's assurances to board members as they rushed to rescue a leader Trump hadn't even heard of when he began his second term.

"The response from the market has been very positive," Trump said in an interview with The Wall Street Journal Monday evening. "That really shows the decision was right." Nvidia stock notched the largest one-day market cap gain on record for a U.S. company.

The behind-the-scenes lobbying was an unprecedented campaign by a U.S. president to bend a company board to his will.

Trump and his team were up against significant crosscurrents. Huang was widely considered to be a political, legal and business liability. Nvidia's board of directors had unanimously accepted his resignation and told investors that he wouldn't return.

But on Monday morning — before the market's opening bell — Nvidia stunned Wall Street and Washington by announcing that the comeback that many in the nation's capital and Silicon Valley had dismissed as a pipe dream was complete.

Nvidia shares quickly recovered much of their roughly 30% decline since Huang's resignation earlier this month, a slide that had dragged down the broader market and fueled fears of a far-reaching contagion. By the close, Nvidia had held its rebound and helped power a rise of 4.7% in the S&P 500.

Shortly after Huang resigned, the president had suggested Nvidia hire former Apple CEO Tim Cook, but became more convinced Huang was the best candidate to lead the chip designer after seeing the market's response and hearing from other executives such as Elon Musk, who helped lead Silicon Valley's support of Huang.

A former venture capitalist, Vance recognized Huang's role as a U.S. champion of open-weight AI models that are cheaper and easier to customize, some of the officials said. That critical role in the race against China's tech sector made Trump and Vance think that reinstating Huang was a priority, the officials said.

On Sunday afternoon, the board met for a marathon session and spent hours talking to Huang, people familiar with the matter said.

Huang disclosed to the board additional affairs beyond the two that had been widely reported, but he was contrite about his behavior, people with knowledge of the discussion said.

After conversations with Huang about the importance of candor and honesty, the board ultimately decided that having him return was the best path, the people said.

When Harvey Jones, chair of the Nvidia board, emailed employees about the news Monday, hearts, thumbs-up, shock, laughing and celebration emojis poured in on Microsoft Outlook.

Huang returned to Nvidia's office on Monday to cheers and shouts of "we love you, Jensen!" from employees, who lined the stairs and balconies of the office to welcome him. Huang, who was wearing a blue zip-up jacket, joked that it was his first day of work and that he didn't have a computer before becoming more serious and thanking his staff.

"I'm terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this," Huang said, according to a video seen by the Journal. "I've made some very terrible mistakes and I'm going to work on coming back."

He added, "Thank you all for this second chance. I'm going to be a better CEO the second time around."

Nvidia said Jones will remain as board chair and interim CEO Colette Kress will continue as chief financial officer. Last week, both said the company wasn't considering bringing Huang back, and Kress had said the company was taking "a strong look" at the types of companies it would help finance, raising concerns about Nvidia's role as the industry's central bank.

The company said its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang.

In the Monday interview with the Journal, Trump said he wanted to call Nvidia's board a week and a half ago. "I'm not sure I would have been as successful," he said. "The climate became more and more right as the company stock began to tumble."

He said he was told the government hadn't found Huang had done anything illegal, only that "he made some indiscretions having to do with other things." Trump said once he heard there was no illegal activity on Huang's part, "I began a push."

The president said he talked to the board "in numerous ways" and "through representatives."

Trump said he called Huang to congratulate him on being reinstated. During the conversation, he said Huang told him about all kinds of new chips he wanted to invent. "There's really nobody like him," the president said.

Trump said he liked getting involved in companies, pointing to the government buying a 10% stake in Intel. "If I can help a company that's got some problems, I do it," he said.

Probes continue

The two-week roller coaster — from the Nvidia board's investigation into Huang to his resignation and subsequent reinstatement — marked an extraordinary comeback for one of the world's most powerful tech leaders. And it signaled that Trump is uncowed in his aggressive and unconventional approach to governance, just weeks after a midterm election that delivered widespread Republican losses driven in part by his unpopularity and voter concerns about AI.

Many national-security questions remain unanswered. The Justice Department is leading two probes of Nvidia customers about suspected chip smuggling, while Nvidia's board investigation continues. Lawmakers are scheduled to hear from Huang next week and have also called for their own investigations.

"It is absurd that Trump intervened before any of the litany of investigations got fully under way," said Gregory Allen, chief executive of Decision Tree Research, a research firm focused on chips and geopolitics.

Nvidia has cooperated for months with the Justice Department investigations into Megaspeed International and Super Micro, a maker of data center servers that has been linked to chip smuggling allegations in the past, the people with direct knowledge said. A former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, is suspected of having worked with Chinese intelligence during an affair with Jensen Huang.

The Commerce Department Monday added Megaspeed and several other firms to the trade blacklist, barring U.S. companies from selling them chips and other technology.

Nvidia's board is sharing information with prosecutors as a committee of independent directors conducts an internal investigation into whether the CEO shared corporate or national security information during his romantic relationship with Alice Huang.

Megaspeed has said it is a compliant company and that it hired outside counsel to investigate the allegations. Super Micro has said it is cooperating with authorities and that it put accused employees on leave. Efforts to reach Alice Huang have been unsuccessful.

After Nvidia's board opened an investigation into Jensen Huang's conduct and potential national-security issues on Nov. 8, Trump stood by him. He said the Nvidia CEO who had lobbied him for licenses to ship older chips directly to China didn't know that Alice Huang was suspected of being a spy, and that he was an amazing guy who had helped keep the U.S. ahead in the tech race.

Trump was briefed at least twice about Alice Huang's connections to Chinese intelligence. In May, he let the Nvidia CEO join his trip to China after Rubio told him about the intelligence community's concerns. The president didn't think the findings warranted action, people familiar with the matter said.

On Nov. 12, Huang resigned following reports of another affair, this one with an executive at Nvidia. Trump suggested Cook could replace Huang on social media, saying "A Legend replaces a Legend!" Kress, the company's chief financial officer, was named interim CEO.

Lawmakers and administration officials fretted over concerns that Nvidia chips were being smuggled directly to China in violation of export control rules. The illicit shipments could help Chinese tech giants like Alibaba and Tencent develop better AI tools that aid the Chinese military, analysts in the industry say.

Many turned their ire on the Commerce Department, which oversees export controls and had stalled actions that would hurt China over the past two years during trade talks. Secretary Howard Lutnick has a close relationship with Trump.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was publicly critical of Commerce, saying that other agencies wanted to add Megaspeed to a trade blacklist but that Commerce blocked the move.

data.title: By Engineering Huang's Return, Trump Endorses Silicon Valley's Founder Mode — WSJ
data.description:
By Tim Higgins

President Trump has decided that in the AI era, some people are too big to fail. That the Imperial CEO must be protected at all costs. That the individual outweighs the institution. That is the message Monday from the president's successful campaign to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia, the AI chip maker at the heart of the technology supporters say will remake the world.

It was only 11 days ago that the Nvidia co-founder was ousted after revelations that he had two extramarital affairs, with a subordinate at the company and a customer who is suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence.

In helping champion Huang's return, Trump further ties his second term — his legacy — to the rise of artificial intelligence and the investment boom around it, even as increasing signs emerge that the market has become overheated.

To keep the AI play alive, Trump is effectively endorsing Founder Mode, the growing dogma within Silicon Valley that founders of companies hold a unique power to create value.

Because of that power, supporters argue, founders should be given special leeway as they pursue growth, innovation and disruption. Their foibles should be overlooked because of the value they create.

"I believe that you have to protect our geniuses," Trump told CNBC shortly after Nvidia's announcement of Huang's return. "We don't have enough of them."

What makes Founder Mode so powerful is that investors largely support the philosophy when the returns go in their favor: Nvidia shares soared more than 30% Monday — after the company had lost about $1 trillion in market value while he was gone.

That Huang's company was under federal investigation didn't appear to matter. ("He did nothing wrong," Trump told CNBC.)

That Huang failed to disclose his indiscretions to the company's board of directors and created an organization full of corporate governance red flags didn't matter. His friends in the New Boys Club — Elon Musk and others in the pro-founder movement — argued the trust he engendered among the industry's delicate supply chain was more important.

That Huang oversaw a company that exploited a gap in U.S. export controls to the benefit of China didn't matter. ("He's in the business of selling chips," Trump said.)

In the end, Huang's biggest problem would seem to be that he lacked a dual-class share structure to protect his power in the first place. Unlike other tech titans, such as Musk at SpaceX and Mark Zuckerberg at Meta Platforms who have a tight grip on corporate decisions by virtue of their ownership stakes, Huang was vulnerable to the pressure of a board jittery about his scandal.

But with powerful friends, like Musk and Trump, even that didn't matter. Last week, Musk argued Huang was irreplaceable — effectively the Michael Jordan of AI.

Trump obviously agreed.

Some supporters argued Huang was critical to ensuring the U.S. remains ahead of China in the race to develop AI. It is a national-security argument that suggests the country is at war for the future — a zero-sum game that is guiding much of the public debate around AI policy.

All important arguments. But the real catalyst for change seemed to be the market selloff.

The president on Monday acknowledged as much and pointed to Huang's unique role in guiding future chip development.

Essentially, he offered Huang as a kind of market bailout.

With the backing of the White House, Huang joins Musk and Zuckerberg among the ranks of other Imperial CEOs. He's now bigger than a board of directors, than shareholders, than the norms of corporate governance. At least, for now, with Trump in power.

data.title: Alice Huang Had Ties to China's Intelligence Network. But Was She Really a Spy? — WSJ
data.description:
By Alexander Ward and Lingling Wei

At the center of the Jensen Huang drama sits a debate over what it means to be a spy.

That definition has shifted in China under Xi Jinping, as the nation's Ministry of State Security has been overhauled to identify and cultivate people with exactly the kind of access Alice Huang had.

The data-industry executive's affair with the Nvidia CEO sparked an international scandal and precipitated Jensen Huang's short-lived exit from his company.

Alice Huang was in contact with Chinese intelligence while the affair was ongoing, according to people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence on the matter. But there was no smoking-gun intelligence proving she had been actively tasked with collecting information on Jensen Huang or passing along national-security secrets, they said.

Some U.S. officials also said the links to Chinese intelligence were circumstantial, given how Chinese business leaders are often compelled to remain in contact with the country's national-security apparatus. Others said the indications that Alice Huang collected and passed on information, regardless of how sensitive, posed a risk to national security given the centrality of Jensen Huang to the U.S. artificial-intelligence industry.

President Trump and his allies highlighted the lack of clarity in the intelligence as they successfully lobbied for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO. In closed-door briefings and TV panel shows, the question of whether Alice Huang was a spy has been perhaps the most fiercely debated issue of the entire scandal.

Interviews with current and former U.S. intelligence officials, lawmakers and China analysts suggest the spy-or-not-a-spy question misses a broader point. The greater challenge, they say, is that China's intelligence services have grown so expansive and opportunistic under Xi that the line between a recruited agent and an unwitting asset has blurred — making it harder to assess the damage and easier to dismiss the threat.

The White House and Central Intelligence Agency declined to comment. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence didn't respond to requests for comment. Beijing has repeatedly denied there was a Chinese plot to spy on Jensen Huang.

Xi's spy machine

The Ministry of State Security has transformed during Xi's tenure from a shadowy, domestically focused agency to what some U.S. intelligence officials now describe as the world's largest and most active spy service, with an estimated 600,000 to 800,000 personnel.

Xi's appointment of his protégé Chen Yixin as minister in 2022 accelerated the expansion. Chen pushed the MSS into the open, launching a WeChat account, producing propaganda videos warning that "foreign spies are everywhere," and amplifying national-security education into school curricula from primary grades through the university level. The message to ordinary Chinese citizens is that everyone is expected to be vigilant, and everyone is a potential participant in the counterespionage effort.

The agency's reach now extends well beyond China's borders. It closely monitors Chinese nationals living overseas, in part through surveillance of WeChat and other digital platforms, and in part through on-the-ground operations. The recruitment of assets abroad also has intensified, with intelligence operatives using LinkedIn-style headhunter approaches, commercial pretexts and face-to-face meetings inside China to cultivate overseas contacts — particularly those with connections to politics, technology, or business.

Against that backdrop, intelligence analysts say Alice Huang would have been impossible for the security service to miss. She was a Chinese businesswoman with direct personal access to the CEO of the world's most strategically important chip-designer — and she posted intimate photos of herself with Jensen Huang on WeChat Moments, visible to anyone in her network.

A warning for Trump

In March, Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a memo to warn Trump about Jensen Huang possibly being compromised by Alice Huang because of her intelligence connections — though the memo didn't definitively say she was a Chinese spy directed to collect intelligence on the Nvidia chief.

In addition to the espionage suspicions, Alice Huang's former company, Singapore-headquartered Megaspeed, has been under investigation by U.S. authorities since at least 2024 for allegedly smuggling restricted Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News earlier this month that it "doesn't matter to me whether she's a spy or not," because the bigger issue is Nvidia's work with companies like Megaspeed to potentially circumvent export restrictions.

Others who favored Huang's reinstatement, including Trump, have suggested the lack of clarity surrounding the nature of Alice Huang's links to Chinese intelligence showed that Nvidia's board was too hasty in moving against Jensen Huang.

Rep. Jim Himes (D., Conn.), the incoming chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, said the U.S. intelligence community doesn't have clear answers on critical questions about Alice Huang, including whether she was an active Chinese agent.

"We need to know what information he conveyed to her, what influence she might have applied to him, whether she was tasked by the Chinese, whether she was witting — we don't know the answer to that question," he said.

The Trump administration hasn't shared much of the underlying intelligence about Alice Huang with Capitol Hill, lawmakers and congressional staff said. A scheduled session to discuss that and other matters last Wednesday was postponed. Jensen Huang is scheduled to appear Dec. 3 before the Senate Banking Committee

In announcing Huang's return, the Nvidia board said that after receiving assurances from senior U.S. officials, it had concluded his "reinstatement poses no national security risk." The company didn't respond to a request for comment.

Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had spoken directly with Xi about Jensen Huang, saying the Chinese leader's respect for the Nvidia CEO was "so great" and that Xi had called him "brilliant." Trump also suggested that if the Nvidia chief were treated badly, he could end up running a rival AI company — in China.

data.title: Japanese Market Sharply Higher; Spikes 4.4%
data.description:
TOKYO (dpa-AFX) - The Japanese stock market is trading sharply higher in post-holiday session on Tuesday, reversing the sharp losses in the previous session, following the broadly positive cues from Wall Street overnight, with the Nikkei 225 jumping 4.4 percent to above the 59,900 level, with gains in across most sectors led by technology and financial stocks.

The markets cheered the reinstatement of AI chipmaker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang and boosted sentiment across the artificial intelligence sector.

The benchmark Nikkei 225 Index is up 2,483.95 points or 4.40 percent at 58,920.60, after touching a high of 59,262.57 earlier. Japanese shares ended sharply lower on Friday ahead of the holiday on Monday.

Market heavyweight SoftBank Group is soaring almost 8 percent and Uniqlo operator Fast Retailing is gaining more than 1 percent. Among automakers, Honda is losing almost 1 percent, while Toyota is gaining almost 1 percent.

In the tech space, Advantest is soaring almost 15 percent, Screen Holdings is surging more than 9 percent and Tokyo Electron is surging more than 12 percent.

In the banking sector, Mitsubishi UFJ Financial is advancing almost 5 percent, Sumitomo Mitsui Financial is gaining almost 4 percent and Mizuho Financial is surging more than 5 percent.

The major exporters are mostly higher. Mitsubishi Electric is advancing almost 7 percent, Panasonic is soaring more than 11 percent and Canon is gaining almost 1 percent, while Sony is edging down 0.4 percent.

Among the other major gainers, Murata Manufacturing and Kokusai Electric are skyrocketing more than 14 percent each, while Resonac Holdings, Taiyo Yuden and Sumco are jumping more than 13 percent each. Lasertec and Furukawa Electric are soaring almost 12 percent each, while Disco is surging more than 11 percent, Renesas Electronics is advancing more than 11 percent and Fujikura is gaining almost 10 percent, while Sumitomo Electric Industries and TDK are adding almost 9 percent each.

Conversely, Dentsu, KDDI, Seven & I Holdings and Rakuten are losing almost 3 percent each.

In economic news, the S&P Global Japan Manufacturing PMI increased to 53.7 in November 2026 from October's seven-month low of 53.3, exceeding market expectations of 53.5, preliminary data showed. Looking ahead, business sentiment remained positive.

Meanwhile, the services PMI Business Activity Index fell to 50.5 in November 2026 from 51.7 in October, marking the weakest expansion in six months.

Japan's S&P Global Composite PMI Business Activity Index eased to 51.5 in November 2026 from a final 52.1 in the previous month, flash data showed, marking the slowest expansion in private-sector activity since May.

In the currency market, the U.S. dollar is trading in the higher 158 yen-range on Tuesday.

On Wall Street, stocks surged during trading on Monday following the sell-off seen over the past several sessions. The major averages have all shown substantial moves back to the upside, with the tech-heavy NASDAQ leading the charge. The major averages opened sharply higher and remained firmly in the green throughout the trading day, ending near session highs.

The major European markets also showed strong moves to the upside as Germany's DAX jumped 2.15 percent, London's FTSE climbed 1.30 percent, the CAC 40 in France improved 1.48 percent and the SMI in Switzerland rose 1.12 percent.

data.title: FireFly Metals Highlights Green Bay Exploration Upside with Second Major Copper-Gold Discovery in a Month
data.description:
FireFly Metals has made a second significant copper-gold discovery in a month at its Green Bay project in the Baie Verte district of north-east Newfoundland in Canada.

Located less than 10 kilometres from the company’s mothballed Ming undergound mine, the Nash volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) discovery was initially identified by an airborne electromagnetic survey completed in 2024.

Follow-up mapping and surface prospecting in the area of a +3km conductive anomaly hosting Nash and the earlier RDI target identified widespread mineralisation in approximately 44 rock chip samples, returning grades as high as 19.8% copper.

Maiden drilling at Nash targeted areas of coincident geophysical and geochemical anomalism, with the results confirming the presence of shallow mineralisation through intersections of 26.7m at 2.3% copper from 9m including a high-grade zone of 9.6m at 4.6%.

The RDI target, located 1.1km from the Nash discovery along the same geophysical trend, returned a maiden shallow intersection of 11.2m at 1.2% copper from 15.9m including 4m at 2.3% after its discovery earlier this month.

Mount Joy System

Firefly identified the high-grade Mount Joy copper-gold system in October after drilling at the previously untested target returned 22.5m at 2.5% copper equivalent from 109m including 9m at 3.9% CuEq.

Mount Joy—which lies 35km east of the Ming mine and 2.6km from the Nugget Pond processing facility, which remains on care and maintenance—emerged from recent airborne electromagnetic surveys, ground-based follow-up work, and geochemical prospecting across the Tilt Cove-Betts Cove VMS district.

At the time, managing director Steve Parsons said the discovery underscored the “immense potential” of the geophysical and geochemical targets identified at Green Bay, supporting a plan to continue driving growth in the project’s mineral resource, mine life, and forecast production rates.

Green Bay Resource

Green Bay’s current mineral resource estimate sits at 60.2 million tonnes grading 2.4% CuEq in the higher confidence Measured and Indicated categories, plus a further 23.5Mt at 2.5% CuEq inferred.

An update is being targeted for early in the new year followed by a feasibility study relating to a 1.8Mt per annum production restart scenario at Ming, which has existing underground access including a decline to 950m and a 650m shaft used for drilling and development.

FireFly has been granted an exclusive option to acquire the contiguous Brass Buckle property less than 10km southeast of Ming.

Brass Buckle comprises 16.5 square kilometres of highly prospective exploration claims immediately adjacent to the Nash discovery.

data.title: Macquarie Led Group to Buy Axiata's International Towers in $1.2 Billion Deal — Update
data.description:
By P.R. Venkat and Ying Xian Wong

A Macquarie-led consortium has agreed to acquire Axiata's international telecom tower businesses, valued at about $1.2 billion, expanding the Australian asset manager's Southeast Asian digital infrastructure footprint.

The consortium will buy the tower businesses of Malaysian telecom group Axiata's unit Edotco in the Philippines, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Cambodia, Macquarie said Monday.

Its Macquarie Asia-Pacific Infrastructure Fund 4 will acquire the Philippine business, which has about 3,200 towers, while other consortium members will buy the rest.

"The investment reflects our conviction in the continued growth of digital infrastructure across Southeast Asia," said Verena Lim, Asia chief executive of Macquarie Group and co-head of Asia-Pacific infrastructure at Macquarie Asset Management.

In a regulatory filing, PT Tower Bersama Infrastructure said it agreed to buy all of Edotco's Indonesian business. Bangladesh-focused private equity firm Osiris Group said it would buy a 70% stake in the Bangladesh business and all of the Pakistan business.

Malaysia's OCK Group said in a filing that it agreed to buy the Cambodia business, which operates more than 3,800 telecom towers.

In its home market, Axiata will also sell about 15.645% of Edotco Malaysia to state fund Khazanah Nasional for about 659.4 million ringgit, equivalent to $159.9 million. Following the deal, Axiata and Khazanah Nasional will each have a 47.355% stake and joint control of the Malaysian business.

The sales are part of a wider restructuring by Axiata that values Edotco at 11.8 billion ringgit.

Axiata expects gross proceeds of about 2.2 billion ringgit, which will mainly be used to pare down debt. The deals are expected to cut its gearing, a measure of debt against equity, to 0.50 times from 0.71 times.

"Reducing leverage and strengthening our balance sheet will give us greater financial and strategic flexibility," Axiata Chief Executive Nik Rizal Kamil said.

The deals need approval from shareholders and regulators. Macquarie expects its purchase to be completed in 2027.

Axiata shares rose as much as 3.0% early Tuesday after the announcement, and were last up 2.4% at 1.71 ringgit.

Analysts were positive on the deal, citing the potential to unlock value from Edotco, reduce Axiata's debt and strengthen its capacity to pay dividends.

The deal marks "tangible progress" on Axiata's long-standing plan to monetize its infrastructure assets, said TA Securities analyst Chan Mun Chun. It would lower Axiata's net debt-to-Ebitda ratio to 1.9 times from 2.5 times, bringing it below management's target of 2.0 times, while unlocking value at an attractive valuation, the analyst said.

CIMB Securities stated the deal would unlock about half of Edotco's value while allowing Axiata to retain its Malaysian tower business for future monetization.

A stronger balance sheet could lower Axiata's risk premium and bolster its dividend-paying capacity, CIMB Securities analysts Choong Chen Foong and Kenny Lim said in a note.

data.title: Two Americans jailed for life by Caribbean court over murder of Canadian entrepreneur, media report
data.description:
By Sarah Peter

Two American men were sentenced to life in prison on the Caribbean island of Dominica on Monday for the 2023 murder of Canadian tech entrepreneur Daniel Langlois and his partner Dominique Marchand, local media reported.

Langlois and Marchand were killed on December 1, 2023, in what the judge described as "an unprovoked attack," saying the case was "the rarest of the rare," according to local media.

The court in the capital, Roseau, gave Jonathan Lehrer and Robert Snyder Jr. two consecutive life sentences each, the reports said.

The pair had been held in custody since their arrest days after the killings and were convicted on July 28 this year. Their lawyer has said they will appeal the sentencing.

Langlois founded Montreal-based Softimage, whose 3-D animation technology was used in major Hollywood productions including "Jurassic Park," "The Matrix" and "Titanic." He and Marchand owned the Coulibri Ridge eco-resort in southern Dominica.

The couple had been missing for several days when their burned bodies were found in a car near Gallion, close to the resort.

Lehrer, a New Jersey-born chocolate maker, owned land next to the resort. Snyder, a mechanic, worked for Lehrer.

Court documents show Lehrer had a years-long dispute with Langlois over a road that crossed his property and led to the resort. In 2019, a judge ordered Lehrer to make the road available to the public and to let Langlois' visitors pass without any limits.

Representatives for Lehrer's family have disputed that the feud over the road was behind the killings.

Last week, family spokesperson Sylvie Deslauriers released a statement on behalf of Langlois' mother. In it, the mother said that her son's ashes had recently been brought back to Canada, where she was able to lay him to rest almost three years after the killings.

HESAI-W disclosed in a filing that the company repurchased shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market and the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on November 20 and Nov 23, respectively.

On November 20, the company repurchased 1.5963 million ADRs of Hesai Group on Nasdaq at prices ranging from USD11.75 to USD12.5 per share, involving approximately USD2.4225 million.

On November 23, the company repurchased 358,900 H shares on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange at prices ranging from HKD11.53 to HKD12 per share, involving approximately HKD4.237 million.

data.title: NVIDIA Partners and Suppliers' Asian Shares Leap; S Korea Stocks Rebound 6%
data.description:
Shares of major Asian partners and suppliers of NVIDIA leapfrogged on Tuesday after CEO Jensen Huang was reinstated by the board, with investors piling back into tech stocks. In South Korea, NVIDIA suppliers Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK Hynix (000660.KS) soared 6% and 8%, respectively.

The two companies together account for more than 40% of the weighting of the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (Kospi), shoring up the index by nearly 6% to lead gains across Asian markets. The rally triggered the Korea Exchange (KRX) to activate its Sidecar mechanism, temporarily suspending program trading buy orders. Reports said this marked the 100th activation of the mechanism by the KRX.

South Korea's LG Electronics (066570.KS) surged 12.86%.

Japan's SoftBank Group , a major investor in the chip sector, climbed more than 3%. Semiconductor testing company Advantest (6657.JP) and peer Tokyo Electron also gained 12% each. Both companies are partners of NVIDIA.

Following Huang's reinstatement, NVIDIA shares closed up 31%. Prior to that, the company's stock had once plunged nearly 33% cumulatively after Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on November 8.

data.title: At AI speed, Nvidia's Jensen Huang finds exoneration
data.description:
Key points:
  • Nvidia shares jump 32% after board announces Huang's reinstatement Monday
  • Trump and Vance pressed Nvidia's board over weekend, people familiar with the matter told Reuters
  • Shareholder suit alleges Nvidia and Huang defrauded investors by concealing alleged relationship

By Greg Bensinger, Deepa Seetharaman, Erin Banco and Steve Holland

In the AI era, everything moves fast.

Jensen Huang's 11-day transformation from persona non grata to prodigal emperor happened before Nvidia began in earnest its investigation into myriad allegations against him, including the executive’s extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese asset. Reuters could not confirm Alice Huang's affiliation with the Chinese government.

Few parallels exist. Walt Disney’s Bob Iger retired in 2020 but came back just two years later before leaving again earlier this year. Among tech firm founders, only Zynga’s Mark Pincus and Workday’s Aneel Bhusri, who both spent about two years away as CEOs, come anywhere close. Steve Jobs spent a dozen years away from Apple . OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's whiplash return from exile in five days in 2023 is an exception.

But none of them were shrouded in as much scandal as Huang’s dizzying fall and rapid exoneration, which came after allegations of multiple affairs, including with subordinates and an executive for a key customer.

The Nvidia board vowed not to reinstate him as recently as Tuesday. But amid pressure from shareholders, venture capitalists and President Donald Trump, Nvidia announced early Monday Huang would once again control the company.

The shares jumped as much as 32% on Monday.

Huang’s initial downfall stemmed from revelations he had a lengthy affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who was a director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company. In the fallout, Reuters reported he had had affairs with two staffers, causing the board to lose confidence in the 63-year-old CEO. He was replaced by Nvidia CFO Colette Kress while the company searched for a permanent successor.

Among the shortlist of candidates, the board reached out, according to reports, to Rene Haas, CEO of Arm , which at 7 a.m. ET (1200 GMT) announced it had extended its contract with Haas through 2033.

Within two hours, Nvidia announced Huang's return.

TURNING A BLIND EYE?

With Nvidia seen as a critical piece of the AI economy, industry executives circled the wagons around the fallen CEO, including on social media and in urgent calls to the board of directors, according to media reports, as Nvidia lost about $1 trillion in market value, casting doubt on the AI trade that had boosted global markets over four years.

University of Washington professor Margaret O'Mara, who writes about the history of technology, said the norm in Silicon Valley has often been to "let this indispensable man do his innovative stuff" and let misbehavior slide. “You can be a brilliant jerk if you can get things done," she said.

Reaction to Jensen Huang’s return was swift.

In addition to Wall Street's elation, Trump praised the board for having “made the correct and proper decision” while taking credit for its U-turn. Elon Musk said on X that “the mistake has been corrected,” and venture capitalists like Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner celebrated the move on social media.

Criticizing the move were elected officials on both sides of the aisle. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said it was “reckless” and the Nvidia board still owed Congress answers about the company’s compliance with US export controls. Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska said Nvidia’s leadership ought to have ignored the Trump administration’s “inexplicable desire to save Huang.”

Meanwhile, Nvidia is facing a shareholder suit alleging the company ⁠and Huang defrauded shareholders ​by concealing Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang. And Reuters reported exclusively last week that Huang misled several of the company's leaders, including its general counsel, about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang.

Huang had apologized for his behavior in an email to Nvidia staff saying, “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do.”

His return contrasts with traditional accountability in corporate America where inter-office affairs with subordinates are disqualifying. Consider the fate of the CEOs of Nestle, BP, Norfolk Southern and Kohl’s, who in just the past three years were all pushed out for inappropriate workplace relationships.

"Accepting the resignation was right," said Nada Kakbadse, Henley Business School professor of corporate governance and ethics, referring to Nvidia. "A relationship with a direct report, plus reports that he misled the general counsel, is a code-of-conduct problem and not a private matter. The reinstatement is the weak decision."

KEY PERSON RISK

Yet, Nvidia is viewed in Washington as critical to the advancement of AI, making Huang’s purgatory, like AI itself, rapid. The Trump administration moved quickly, playing a singular role in Huang’s return.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance over the weekend were personally engaged with Nvidia’s board to pressure them to reinstate Huang, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also played roles in determining Jensen Huang was not a security risk to the US and did not see any evidence that he did anything illegal or untoward related to US national security, these people said.

In conversations over the weekend, administration and White House officials debated whether there could be a national security crisis because he personally held relationships with supply chain companies deemed critical, one of the people said.

The Nvidia CEO, the White House said, had been unaware that Alice Huang had any affiliations with the Chinese state, one person told Reuters.

So, despite its assurances that it would seek a new leader, the Nvidia board reversed its decision and announced his reinstatement Monday morning. “Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA,” said board chairman Harvey Jones.

Huang returned to Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters Monday to cheers from staffers, who chanted his name. “I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you all through all of this,” he said.

data.title: Macquarie Led Group to Buy Axiata's International Towers in $1.2B Deal — Update
data.description:
By P.R. Venkat and Ying Xian Wong

A Macquarie-led consortium has agreed to acquire Axiata's international telecom tower businesses, valued at about $1.2 billion, expanding the Australian asset manager's Southeast Asian digital infrastructure footprint.

The consortium will buy the tower businesses of Malaysian telecom group Axiata's unit Edotco in the Philippines, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Cambodia, Macquarie said Monday.

Its Macquarie Asia-Pacific Infrastructure Fund 4 will acquire the Philippine business, which has about 3,200 towers, while other consortium members will buy the rest.

"The investment reflects our conviction in the continued growth of digital infrastructure across Southeast Asia," said Verena Lim, Asia chief executive of Macquarie Group and co-head of Asia-Pacific infrastructure at Macquarie Asset Management.

In a regulatory filing, PT Tower Bersama Infrastructure said it agreed to buy all of Edotco's Indonesian business. Bangladesh-focused private equity firm Osiris Group said it would buy a 70% stake in the Bangladesh business and all of the Pakistan business.

Malaysia's OCK Group said in a filing that it agreed to buy the Cambodia business, which operates more than 3,800 telecom towers.

In its home market, Axiata will also sell about 15.645% of Edotco Malaysia to state fund Khazanah Nasional for about 659.4 million ringgit, equivalent to $159.9 million. Following the deal, Axiata and Khazanah Nasional will each have a 47.355% stake and joint control of the Malaysian business.

The sales are part of a wider restructuring by Axiata that values Edotco at 11.8 billion ringgit.

Axiata expects gross proceeds of about 2.2 billion ringgit, which will mainly be used to pare down debt. The deals are expected to cut its gearing, a measure of debt against equity, to 0.50 times from 0.71 times.

"Reducing leverage and strengthening our balance sheet will give us greater financial and strategic flexibility," Axiata Chief Executive Nik Rizal Kamil said.

The deals need approval from shareholders and regulators. Macquarie expects its purchase to be completed in 2027.

Axiata shares rose as much as 3.0% early Tuesday after the announcement, and were last up 2.4% at 1.71 ringgit.

Analysts were positive on the deal, citing the potential to unlock value from Edotco, reduce Axiata's debt and strengthen its capacity to pay dividends.

The deal marks "tangible progress" on Axiata's long-standing plan to monetize its infrastructure assets, said TA Securities analyst Chan Mun Chun. It would lower Axiata's net debt-to-Ebitda ratio to 1.9 times from 2.5 times, bringing it below management's target of 2.0 times, while unlocking value at an attractive valuation, the analyst said.

CIMB Securities stated the deal would unlock about half of Edotco's value while allowing Axiata to retain its Malaysian tower business for future monetization.

A stronger balance sheet could lower Axiata's risk premium and bolster its dividend-paying capacity, CIMB Securities analysts Choong Chen Foong and Kenny Lim said in a note.

data.title: China, HK stocks rebound from one-year lows as Nvidia comeback lifts AI shares
data.description:
China and Hong Kong stocks rebounded on Tuesday from more than one-year lows, as Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO sparked a rally in AI-related shares and helped reverse part of last week's global equity selloff.

The move marked a sharp turnaround in market sentiment after leadership turmoil at the world's most valuable chipmaker and renewed concerns over AI spending had rattled global markets in recent sessions.

China's blue-chip CSI300 Index opened up 1.2%, while the Shanghai Composite Index rose 0.8% after hitting its lowest level since July 2025 on Monday.

The tech-focused STAR50 Index jumped 3.3%, while the 5G Communication Index surged 7%. Memory-chip giant CXMT rose more than 6%.

Hong Kong's benchmark Hang Seng Index opened up 1.1%, after falling to its weakest level since April 2025 on Monday. The Hang Seng Artificial Intelligence Index opened up 6%.

South Korea's KOSPI rose more than 7%, while Japan's Nikkei gained nearly 5% in early trade.

data.title: Oil prices hold decline amid cautious optimism over West Asia peace efforts
data.description:
Oil prices steadied post sliding over 3% in the prior session on cautious optimism over efforts to end the West Asia war.

Brent crude was near $89 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate was about $80 a barrel.

US Vice-President JD Vance met Qatar's prime minister to discuss the negotiations with Iran, Bloomberg reported, citing Axios. The Persian Gulf nation has acted as a mediator in efforts to resolve the conflict that is nearing nine months.

Global benchmark brent declined this month after US President Donald Trump held off on renewed strikes post the Democratic sweep of the US midterm polls, although there has been a rise in low-level fighting. Trump recently threatened attacks would resume next year if talks failed.

Despite the hostilities, including frequent attacks on tankers transiting via the Strait of Hormuz, crude exports from the Persian Gulf have increased. The International Energy Agency has estimated the market to swing to a surplus this quarter, while Goldman Sachs has flagged a possible glut next year, Bloomberg reported.

While hope of a negotiated settlement remains, major differences between the US and Iran continue. Tehran wants the US naval blockade of its ports to be lifted, sanctions to be eased and frozen assets to be released before it entirely opens the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Washington is demanding concessions related to Iran's nuclear programme.
